World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Iran ready for 'renewed' hostilities as Trump cools on peace proposal
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he will review a new Iranian peace proposal, but has cast doubt over its prospects as he left open the possibility of future attacks on Iran.

Negotiations between the two countries have been deadlocked since a ceasefire came into effect on April 8, with one round of peace talks during the two-month war having failed in Pakistan.

The dour outlook came after Iran's Tasnim and Fars news agencies reported Tehran submitted a 14-point proposal to mediators in Islamabad.

Details included ending the conflict on all fronts and enacting a new framework for the crucial Strait of Hormuz, Tasnim said.

Mr Trump says his main priority is preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

"I will soon be reviewing the plan that Iran has just sent to us, but can't imagine that it would be acceptable in that they have not yet paid a big enough price for what they have done to Humanity, and the World, over the last 47 years," Mr Trump said on his Truth Social platform.

In a brief interview with reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, he declined to specify what could trigger new military action against the Islamic Republic.

"If they misbehave, if they do something bad, but right now, we'll see," Mr Trump said.

"But it's a possibility that could happen, certainly."

Mohammad Jafar Asadi, a senior figure in the Iranian military's central command, said that "renewed conflict between Iran and the United States is likely."

Iran and US in 'game of chicken' There are duelling narratives from Iran and US about the economic pressures of the war, so will the blockade get negotiations going?

"Evidence has shown that the United States is not committed to any promises or agreements," he added, according to Fars news agency.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told diplomats in Tehran, "The ball is in the United States' court to choose the path of diplomacy or the continuation of a confrontational approach."

Iran, he said, was "prepared for both paths."

Loading...

'Hypocritical behaviour'

US news site Axios reported earlier in the week that Mr Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff, had asked for Tehran's nuclear program to be put back on the negotiating table.

Iran's mission to the UN pointed to the massive US nuclear arsenal, accusing Washington on Saturday of "hypocritical behaviour" towards Iran's own atomic ambitions.

In recent weeks, very few ships have managed to transit the Strait of Hormuz due to Iran's closure of the strait and the US blockade. (Reuters)

There was no legal "restriction on the level of uranium enrichment, so long as it is conducted under the IAEA's supervision, as was the case with Iran," it said, using the abbreviation for the UN nuclear watchdog.

Iran has maintained a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, choking off major flows of oil, gas and fertiliser to the world economy, while the United States has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

Oil prices are about 50 per cent above pre-war levels.

The vice speaker of Iran's parliament, Ali Nikzad, said that under draft legislation being considered for managing the waterway, 30 per cent of tolls collected would go towards military infrastructure, with the rest earmarked for "economic development."

"Managing the Strait of Hormuz is more important than acquiring nuclear weapons," Mr Nikzad said.

Meanwhile, fighting continued on Saturday (local time) in Lebanon, where Israel has carried out deadly strikes despite a separate truce with the Iran-backed armed group Hezbollah.

The Israeli military said it had struck dozens of Hezbollah targets across southern Lebanon following evacuation warnings for nine villages.

While the US and Iranian ceasefire has held, Israel has continued to strike Lebanon despite the two countries also declaring a ceasefire. (Reuters: Karamallah Daher)

Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported three deaths in the attacks.

Hezbollah, for its part, claimed several attacks targeting Israeli troops.

The Israeli strikes included one in the village of Yaroun on what its military called a "religious building," which was damaged.

The French Catholic charity L'Oeuvre d'Orient said the troops had "destroyed" a convent belonging to the Salvatorian Sisters, a Greek-Catholic religious order with which the charity is affiliated.

Iran executes accused spies

Another two men were executed after they were accused of spying for Israel, including one accused of gathering intelligence near the Natanz nuclear site in central Isfahan province, Iranian media reported.

They quoted the judiciary as saying Yaghoub Karimpour and Nasser Bakarzadeh were hanged after being found guilty of intelligence cooperation with Israel and its spy agency, Mossad.

They said Mr Karimpour passed sensitive information to a Mossad officer, while Mr Bakarzadeh was accused of collecting details on government and religious figures and key sites, including in the Natanz area.

The UN has estimated that more than 24 people have been executed in Iran since the war started, with thousands more arrested. (Reuters/WANA: Majid Asgaripour)

Another man was executed for the alleged involvement in the killing of a security officer, the judiciary's news outlet Mizan reported, after the Supreme Court upheld his sentence in late 2025.

The defendant, identified as Mehrab Abdollahzadeh, was described as one of the main individuals responsible for the death of security officer Abbas Fatemiyeh, killed in 2022 during a nationwide protest movement sparked by the death of a young woman, Mahsa Amini, in police custody.

Killing of journalists highlights the impunity with which Israel acts According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, the Israel Defense Forces have committed more targeted killings of journalists than any other government's military since 1992.

Mizan said the defendant confessed to assaulting the security officer.

Rights group HRANA quoted an informed source as saying Mr Abdollahzadeh was subject to torture to extract forced confessions.

According to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Iran has executed more than 24 people and arrested more than 4,000 since the Middle East war began.

Iran's economic toll

In Washington, politicians were wrestling over whether Mr Trump had breached a deadline to seek congressional approval for the war.

Administration officials argue the ceasefire paused a 60-day clock, after which congressional authorisation would be required — a claim disputed by opposition Democrats.

The Israel Defense Forces continue to operate in southern Lebanon and strikes have occurred in this region on an almost daily basis. (Reuters: Shir Torem)

Can OPEC survive without the UAE? The United Arab Emirates's decision to pull the plug on its OPEC membership could be the nail in the coffin for an organisation that has struggled to keep its members in line for the past 66 years.

In Iran, the war's economic toll is deepening, with oil exports crimped and inflation surging past 50 per cent.

"Everyone is trying to endure it, but … they are falling apart," 40-year-old Tehran resident Amir said.

"We still have not seen much of the economic effects because everyone had a bit of savings. They had some gold and dollars for a rainy day. When they run out, things will change."

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Mercury would 'be alive': Shark victim's family welcomes new drone plan
World.content:
The twin brother of shark attack victim, Mercury Psillakis, says he would still be alive if drones had been monitoring Long Reef Beach in Sydney's north on that fatal day in September last year.

Mike Psillakis, along with his brother's widow, Maria, joined authorities in announcing community-led surveillance that will see surfers from local clubs trained in operating the devices to ensure year-round protection.

By the end of winter, it is expected there will be 125 new drone pilots and an extra 60 drones, emblazoned with a message to Merc, in skies between Newcastle and Wollongong.

Surfers will be trained to operate drones as part of a shark surveillance program. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

The renowned surfer died a day before Father's Day in 2025 from catastrophic injuries after he was mauled by a great white shark. He was 57 years old.

Mr Psillakis described what happened to his brother as "extraordinary", saying the family was appreciative of the moves to protect surfers.

"I believe on the sixth of September, if there was a drone in the sky that day, Mercury will still be with us," he said.

"So that's a great step in the right direction, and it'll be an ongoing journey."

Mercury Psillakis (right) with his twin brother Mike. (Supplied)

Surveillance after patrol season ends

The initiative, an expansion of NSW's $30 million Shark Management Program, is in partnership with Surfing NSW and taps into its $650,000 funding package from the Minns government.

It also complements the work of Surf Life Saving NSW, but will fill in the gaps by operating beyond the end of patrol season, in recognition that clubs run events all-year round.

The training will also focus on helping pilots identify high-risk species, with protocols in place in the event of a shark sighting, which includes pausing events for a minimum of 30 minutes.

Surfing NSW is responsible for training the new drone pilots. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Ms Psillakis said it was an honour that so many people cared about her husband and wanted to uphold his legacy.

Adding that while it was upsetting that he wasn't present, he would be proud "that he's somewhat responsible for extra safety on our beaches".

"The release of these drones in Mercury's name is deeply, deeply meaningful to us and our family.

"We are truly grateful for the commitment shown here to innovation, to safety, to protecting those who share our coastline.

"These drones represent progress. They represent the lives that may be saved, families that may be spared this unimaginable loss."

Loading...

'Shark nets don't work'

Minister for Agriculture and Regional NSW Tara Moriarty said the government had embraced the technology as it meant that beaches did not have to be closed all day, but could reopen when sharks had moved on.

But she acknowledged they had to keep looking forward as the technology was quickly evolving.

"We're looking at what we're going to continue to resource for next summer and the summers into the future," she said.

"We'll continue to work with the sector and the experts on the best use of technology to be able to spot sharks faster.

"The shark nets are here to stay for the moment."

The NSW government says it has embraced the new technology. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

For Mr Psillakis however, the time for shark nets is over along with "old ways of thinking".

"My experience is that there were shark nets in place when he [Mercury] was taken. So in my experience, shark nets don't work," he said.

Shark victim's twin brother leads paddle out The twin brother of shark victim Mercury Psillakis has led hundreds of surfers in a paddle out in his memory on Sydney's Northern Beaches.

"Personally, I'd like to see AI drone technology because it's not just the contest surfers on the weekends, it's citizens that surf during the morning, before work and in the afternoons that I want protected," he said.

"I want a box launch from sunrise to sunset, totally automated, where you don't have to have a man pilot.

"I'd like to see the shark populations looked at as well, because that's something that's not really discussed."

Training started for surfers in the Northern Beaches on Saturday, with sessions expected to take place across southern beaches after that.

Two regional courses are also scheduled to take place.

World.title: Firefighters who died battling blaze, from cancer added to honour roll
World.content:
Hundreds of people have honoured the families and legacies of Western Australia's fallen firefighters at a memorial service in Kings Park on Sunday.

Three names were added to the Fallen Firefighters' Honour Roll, which includes volunteer and career firefighters who have died in the line of duty or as a consequence of their service.

Wreaths has been laid to honour the fallen firefighters. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

West River Bush Fire Service volunteer firefighter of 27 years, Gregory Mark Mudie, died while battling a fire near Ravensthorpe, in December last year.

Career firefighter Damian Keiran Buswell, who worked in Welshpool and Albany, dedicated 32 years to emergency services and died from cancer in 2022.

Damian Buswell served as a district manager in the Southern Region for some periods of time. (Supplied)

Denis Jung first joined the Carnarvon Volunteer Fire and Rescue Service in 2001 and later served as an aviation firefighter at Perth Airport.

Denis Jung joined the fire service as a volunteer in 2001. (Supplied)

He also died of cancer in 2022, at the age of 39.

Under WA's Presumptive Legislation, it is presumed that a current or retired firefighter diagnosed with any of a list of 20 cancers acquired it in relation to their duties.

The legislation was introduced so firefighters can access financial support for their treatment, but it guides the addition of names to the Fallen Firefighters' Honour Roll.

Minister for Emergency Services Paul Papalia said there are now 103 names on the honour roll, and the Firefighters' Memorial in Kings Park.

Hundreds of people attended and paid their respects at the service. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"Names of individuals who made the ultimate sacrifice on behalf of their friends, family and community," he said.

" We will remember them. "

Emergency Services commissioner Darren Klemm told the crowd that the fallen firefighters were remembered with deep respect for their courage and commitment

"It's important that our first responders continue to stand together and support each other through these times of loss," he said.

Farmer killed in bushfire identified A farmer who died trying to stop a "treacherous" fire from destroying his family's property in WA's south is identified as the local town's deputy shire president.

"While the pain of losing someone will never truly leave, families can take pride in their loved ones' service and the legacy that they leave behind.

"We will continue to honour those who have fallen, and stand with the families they leave behind."

The next of kin of the fallen firefighters were presented with a medallion honouring their service.

The annual service is held as part of International Firefighter's Day, at the Firefighters' Memorial Grove in Kings Park.

Nominations for the Fallen Firefighters' Honour Roll can be made at any time to the Department of Fire and Emergency Services.

World.title: Sister shares memories of 24yo climber Angela Ha who died at Arapiles
World.content:
Angela Ha's younger sister Michelle remembers her as "the fun" in their family: warm, ruthlessly positive and endlessly adventurous.

Angela, 24, lost her life after falling while rock climbing at Organ Pipes at Mount Arapiles in western Victoria about 11:30am on Monday, April 27.

She died later at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne, 50 minutes before Michelle and their father Daniel arrived from Sydney.

Angela Ha (left) and her sister Michelle (right) were best friends. (Supplied: Michelle Ha)

'The centre of her world'

Michelle said Angela began climbing about five years ago. It quickly became, in Michelle's words, "the centre of her world".

As a child, Angela and her sibling were always active. They ran in cross-country, played soccer and competed at athletics.

But Michelle said climbing gave Angela a true sense of purpose.

Angela Ha's loved ones remember her as warm, adventurous and positive. (Supplied: Michelle Ha)

"She was always a go-getter," Michelle said.

"Never sitting still, trying out new things constantly and loving everything.

"She always loved nature, loved animals, loved friends, but when she did start rock climbing it really started to shape who she was as a person."

Michelle laughed recalling the one attempt she made at following Angela up a cliff.

"I went up once and I came straight back down," Michelle said.

"But she was a great teacher and I was glad I got up there."

Older sister, best friend

To Michelle, Angela was an older sister and a best friend. The person she did everything with.

Michelle said Angela's presence felt like a "warm hug".

She said people gravitated to Angela because she made everyone feel "nothing but comfortable".

The sisters often spoke about Angela's adventures: a new trail, a new route, a new country.

Angela and Michelle Ha celebrate their birthdays five days apart each February. (Supplied: Michelle Ha)

There is a gap of three years between Angela, the oldest sibling, and Michelle, who is 21. And they have two more younger siblings: Stephanie (15) and Marcus (13).

Michelle and Angela were both born in February.

"I think it's only been one year out of my 21 years of living that I haven't celebrated my birthday with her next to me," Michelle said.

"I won't have her physically there to celebrate every year anymore."

Their parents, Daniel and Ruby, weren't ready to speak and asked Michelle to take on that responsibility.

Dedicated to climbing

Angela was a strong climber. Her work ethic in the sport paralleled her academic success.

She completed a Bachelor of Architecture at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) in 2023.

After taking a gap year in 2024, she began a Doctorate of Physiotherapy at the University of Sydney.

When she was younger, Angela wanted to be an architect.

After falling in love with rock climbing, her goal shifted. She decided she wanted to become someone who could help rock climbers heal after injury.

'I got to see her one last time'

Angela was several days into a 10-day expedition with UNSW friends when she fell.

Angela Ha climbing at Mount Arapiles hours before her fall on Monday. (Supplied: Michelle Ha)

Police and Ambulance Victoria said emergency services were called to Mount Arapiles on Monday morning.

SES volunteers climbed with paramedics to reach Angela on the wall.

Later, advanced life support crew and mobile intensive care paramedics winched Angela to an ambulance helicopter, moving her to a nearby paddock where she was treated for more than an hour.

Michelle was in Sydney when she received a call from Angela's close friend, Margot.

Michelle had only met Margot once and knew immediately the call would be about something bigger than "a couple of bumps or a graze".

" I was in the city on the light rail and I grabbed my little sister and said we had to go home. "

She spoke with more of Angela's friends who were at the crag when she fell and they told Michelle she had been moving, scratching her arms and nose occasionally, after the fall.

"Angela has had injuries and she's always been able to make it through," Michelle said.

Michelle and her father Daniel booked the next flight to Melbourne to see Angela in hospital.

Angela's mother Ruby stayed at home in Sydney, caring for her youngest children.

Angela died at 9:40pm on Monday.

Michelle and Daniel arrived at the hospital less than an hour later.

They sat with Angela for about 5 hours, talking to her and holding her hand.

"I'm glad I got to see her one last time," Michelle said.

Rock climbing was the centre of Angela Ha's world, Michelle says. (Supplied: Michelle Ha)

Honouring her

Angela's family has raised more than $60,000 on GoFundMe to celebrate Angela's life.

Michelle said the family had barely discussed the money.

"Dad was saying the numbers [money] didn't really mean much to him," Michelle said.

"He is very appreciative and grateful but the fact over 600 people have shown support and love to Angela, he has been ecstatic about that.

"I just want everyone to live their life, to live their daily life to the fullest. In doing so, it's very much honouring her."

World.title: Man, 18, dies after car rolls over on Perth's Mitchell Freeway
World.content:
A young man has died in a horrific car accident that occurred this morning, forcing the Mitchell Freeway northbound between Southport and Powis streets to close.

Confirming an investigation was underway, Western Australian police said a white Nissan Patrol station sedan was travelling northbound on the Mitchell Freeway at about 10:30am when the driver lost control of the vehicle near the Powis Street exit, causing it to roll.

"The 18-year-old male driver, who was the sole occupant of the vehicle, sustained critical injuries and was conveyed to Royal Perth Hospital, where sadly he died a short time later," police said in a statement.

Heavy traffic is seen on the northbound Mitchell Freeway as police investigate. (Supplied: Main Roads WA. )

Officers from the Major Crash Investigation Section are examining the scene and appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident to report it to Crime Stoppers.

In a social media post, Main Roads WA has urged Perth drivers to seek an alternative route, with heavy traffic reported far back in Hay Street.

World.title: Albanese readies federal budget to favour gen Z and millennial voters
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is preparing to break an election commitment and overhaul property tax perks in this month's budget, to give younger Australians a "fair crack" at owning their own homes.

Albanese's second term was rewritten by events One year ago, Anthony Albanese was a man on top of the world.

In an interview with the ABC to mark one year since Labor's landslide victory, Mr Albanese said he would "absolutely" lead Labor to a third election in 2028.

Conscious that gen Z and millennials now outnumber Baby Boomers at the ballot box, the government is widely tipped to use its upcoming budget to wind back negative gearing and the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount, which have both encouraged investors into the market.

There is growing speculation Labor will also increase the tax paid on distributions from family trusts, as part of a package of measures to be finalised by cabinet in the coming days.

Mr Albanese did not rule out "grandfathering" existing investment properties from the changes, when asked.

"I want Australia to be a land of opportunity for the future and the truth is, young people feel like they're not getting a fair crack at the moment," Mr Albanese told the ABC.



"So any changes we put in the budget, or indeed while we're in government, will be very much focused on those principles."

Before the last election, Mr Albanese ruled out changes to negative gearing, used by about 1.1 million landlords, telling reporters the policy was "off the table".

Since then, the government has sought to reframe the debate by talking up the need to address the intergenerational inequality and help younger Australians get into the property market.

The government is widely tipped to use its upcoming budget to wind back negative gearing. (ABC News: John Gunn)

When asked if making changes to negative gearing was worth the risk of breaking another election promise, Mr Albanese said "voters will make their decisions".

Melbourne, Sydney record biggest house price falls Momentum in the housing market has slowed.

"My job and the job of the government is to put in place measures that are in the interests of the Australian public, not just to make the easy decisions but to make the hard decisions that are in the national interest," he said.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said he was "dead against" any tax increases but indicated he would consider any proposals put forward by the government on May 12.

"All we have seen from budget leaks is that the government wants to tax Australians more. And we're dead set against that," Senator Canavan told Insiders.

"When you put to me specific options, look, I'll consider them. But what I want to see is tax rates go down."

In an interview with the ABC, Mr Albanese said he would "absolutely" lead Labor to the next election, by which time he would have surpassed Paul Keating's record as prime minister.

"I'm certainly motivated; I'm captain of a very strong team," he said.

World.title: By-election of no consequence leaves some major party insiders disturbed
World.content:
Victorians Liberals are breathing a sigh of relief.

When Opposition Leader Jess Wilson was first confronted by the reality that Liberal MP Sam Groth's resignation from parliament would force a by-election on the Mornington Peninsula, she declared she was "excited by the opportunity".

That opportunity threatened to become a nightmare, with a surging One Nation and determined independent Tracee Hutchison challenging the status quo and potentially derailing any momentum Wilson had gathered in the lead-up to the November general election.

The Liberals's Anthony Marsh has won, but One Nation did win a quarter of the vote and that should sound alarm in Labor, Liberal and Nationals headquarters.

One Nation and independent Tracee Hutchison presented a challenge for the Liberal Party. (ABC News)

In the days leading up to Saturday's poll, Liberal MPs and insiders were preparing for a long night, and potentially days, of painstaking vote counting.

Expectations were being lowered.

It was a genuine fear that the party would lose a lot of the primary vote and the most pessimistic were worried the seat would fall to One Nation's Darren Hercus.

The Liberals' primary vote did drop 9.6 per cent. If this were to happen in November, the quest to topple the government would fail.

"We know we have lessons to learn from last night's result; we know we have more to do every day between now and the election to earn the trust of Victorians,'' Wilson said on Sunday.

Liberal insiders feared One Nation's Darren Hercus would beat Anthony Marsh to take the seat of Nepean. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

It's a view shared by MPs and party strategists.

But this was a by-election of no consequence, and a contest that the governing Labor party did not enter.

However, as Wilson says, there are lessons.

November's state election is likely to be tough for the two major parties; this by-election has proved that.

One in four voters in Nepean supported One Nation, and in some areas, such as Rosebud and Dromana, with more working-class voters, it was even higher.

It's a warning for the major parties, one that has left some party operatives "disturbed" about what might happen in November.

"In Nepean, that working-class profile is geographically contained,'' pollster and former Labor party strategist Kosmos Samaras said on Saturday night.

"In dozens of other seats, held by Labor, the Liberals and the Nationals alike, it is far more prolific.

" Tonight is a preview of what the Victorian election in November may look like. "

A former Labor strategist says working-class voters have sent the major parties a warning ahead of the state election in November. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

He warned both sides were going to lose skin, but the risk was greater for the Coalition.

It makes the Liberals's path to government even more perilous. One Nation will be a hindrance in some seats and helpful in others for the Coalition.

It's partly why Labor is ramping up its rhetoric to paint One Nation and the Coalition as allies.

"The result from Nepean is crystal clear that the Liberal Party can't govern without One Nation; they are going to be relying on One Nation and that is something Victorians can't afford,'' Premier Jacinta Allan said on Sunday.

Liberals are also pleased the independent Hutchison didn't attract more votes, especially among wealthier voters. She still secured 21.3 per cent of the primary vote and is likely to finish second after preferences.

It's another sign of a fragmented electorate: one fed up with major parties.

Independent Tracee Hutchison attracted more than a fifth of primary votes. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"They want to send the major parties a message, they want us to listen to them,'' Wilson said. "I get it."

Wilson's leadership helped stem the tide in Nepean, and she continues to make the Coalition competitive.

"They have a leader that is performing well and preventing the roof from falling on top of them,'' Samaras said.

Former Labor strategist Kosmos Samaras says the Nepean results are good news for Liberal leader Jess Wilson. (ABC News)

Labor didn't run, a decision the result vindicates.

It has a swag of its own problems to confront: the premier's popularity levels, crime rates and the cost of living.

But it is talking about positive policies now with the rollout of its budget.

Liberal MPs have noted that while they are focusing on negatives and one by-election, Labor MPs are talking to their electorates about new funds and programs.

In the final days of the Nepean campaign Wilson turned up the volume on the Coalition's anger at Victoria's historic treaty with First Peoples, which the opposition will rip up.

It was a deliberate choice, and it was firmly aimed at voters considering One Nation.

A sign authorised by the Liberal Party at a Nepean polling booth on Saturday. (ABC News)

As One Nation grows, so too will scrutiny.

But highlighting problems with One Nation policies doesn't necessarily mean voters will drop their support. Part of the appeal of Pauline Hanson's party is that it a vote against the political establishment.

Labor is happy to take on One Nation, whereas the Liberals are treading much more cautiously.

Wilson on Sunday refused to comment on where they would preference One Nation in November.

As the premier said, the Coalition may need One Nation's help to change the government.

Many Liberals share the sentiment that a win is a win. And sometimes winning is all that matters.

This will boost the party's confidence that it is on the right track, while also reminding the Coalition that is has lots of work to do if it is to change the government.

It will require the Coalition to win at least 16 seats, without losing any, and in this new fragmented political environment all parties are on notice.

World.title: Live: Suns kick away after half-time as King recovers from huge clash
World.content:
The GWS Giants burst to life after a slow start at Carrara Stadium, as Gold Coast's Ben King is left worse for wear after a big marking contest.

Earlier, Malcolm Rosas Jr kicked a career-high seven goals as Sydney held off a fast-finishing Melbourne at the SCG as Brodie Grundy starred in his 250th game.

Elsewhere in the AFL, scans have confirmed St Kilda star Max King is set for another stint on the sidelines, this time due to a hamstring injury.

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

Key Events HT: Gold Coast 4.8 (32) leads GWS Giants 3.10 (28) 36 minutes ago QT: Gold Coast 3.4 (22) leads GWS Giants 1.7 (13) 1 hours ago Play underway between the Suns and Giants 1 hours ago Show all key events AFL Sunday Scoreboard L By Luke Pentony Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 93 Key Events 12 Goals 47 Suns vs Giants 26 Swans vs Demons 59 Comments 1 All filters Gothard gets a goal out of nowhere for the Giants C By Chris De Silva Phoenix Gothard gets a much-needed goal for GWS! He gets on the hand of a lovely little handball from Harvey Thomas and snaps it home off one bounce. He's very lucky he's gotten a good bounce there because that ball was so very close to the right-hand goal post. There's a bit of a wait to see whether the ARC needs to check this, and Gothard nervously tugs onto the top of his jumper as he waits, but it's eventually awarded. Jamarra has his second for the quarter, GWS in danger zone C By Chris De Silva Jamarra Ugle-Hagan is making his presence felt in this third quarter! It's a long ball inside 50 and Jamarra ghosts in from the side of a big pack of players and ends up taking the grab relatively uncontested. He goes back and drills the set shot from directly in front to give Gold Coast a handy 23-point lead. Petracca grabs his second after forward 50 stoppage C By Chris De Silva Christian Petracca with a terrific spinning finish, and suddenly the Suns are out to a 17-point lead! Gold Coast has a throw-in deep inside its attacking 50, and it's a messy old ball bobbling about after the ruck contest. Petracca smartly stays a little outside of the immediate contest and waits for the ball to bobble out and then he swoops on it, spins out of trouble and snaps on goal, all in one motion. What a goal. What a player. Petracca's now got 19 disposals, eight score involvements, six inside 50s, four clearances and two goals. Three Brownlow votes anyone? Jamarra goals after perfect bounce C By Chris De Silva The Suns strike first after half-time and it's through Jamarra Ugle-Hagan! Jamarra plays the role of the rover after a marking contest in the pocket, and snaps on his trusty left boot. Lachie Whitfield looks like he's got the ball covered in the goalsquare, but the ball takes a wicked bounce straight over his head and through the big sticks! King with a rare miss to start third term C By Chris De Silva A lovely bit of transition out of the back half from the Suns results in a set shot for Ben King 30m out from goal on a slight angle. King usually gobbles this up, but hits the left-hand goalpost this time. King is now 27.7 for the season. Just an incredible conversion rate. The second half is underway at Carrara Stadium C By Chris De Silva Noah Anderson standing shoulder-to-shoulder with Clayton Oliver at the first bounce to begin the third term. I wonder whether the Suns will apply any sort of tag to Oliver, given the dominant first half he had. HT: Gold Coast 4.8 (32) leads GWS Giants 3.10 (28) C By Chris De Silva Christian Petracca (left) had 15 disposals in the first half against the Giants. (Getty Images) Players from both sides looking absolutely GASSED at the half-time siren in sapping conditions. The Suns take a four-point lead into the half-time break courtesy of the late goal to Ben King. It's been a real war of attrition this one, and the dewy conditions haven't made for good kicking in front of goal with a lot of balls sliding off the side of the boot. The Suns lead the inside 50 count 30-22 and the Giants lead the clearance count 18-16. The tackles are virtually dead even, with the Giants holding a 33-32 lead. Clayton Oliver has been sensational in the first half and leads all players with 20 disposals to go along with six clearances and five score involvements. John Noble is Gold Coast's leading ball-winner with 18 disposals and has a game-high 447m gained with four rebound 50s. Finn Callaghan's also had an excellent half, tallying 18 disposals, six score involvements and four tackles. It's not been a night for the key forwards so far, unless you're Aaron Cadman. Cadman's got two goals and has nine disposals and four marks, but Jamarra Ugle-Hagan, Ben King and Jesse Hogan have all combined for nine touches. King gets on the board after Petracca's brilliant pick-up C By Chris De Silva Ben King has his first goal of the night and the Giants are back in front! Kieran Briggs drops an intercept mark that he probably should've gobbled up, and you can't do that around Christian Petracca. Petracca swoops in, picks up the ball with one hand off the ground and then hands off to Ben King, who snaps truly on the left boot under a little bit of pressure. That's Gold Coast's first goal of the quarter after 12 inside 50s. Gothard puts the Giants in front! C By Chris De Silva The Suns chance their arm once again and it pays off handsomely! Another aggressive kick into the corridor, and it eventually ends in the hands of Phoenix Gothard, who takes an uncontested mark inside 50, and then plays on to kick the goal. The Giants have kicked three goals in a row now after the Suns kicked the opening three. Hardwick might break another window in the box if things keep going like this. Cadman drills set shot to draw Giants closer C By Chris De Silva Geez, this kid is going to be a star isn't he? Aaron Cadman with a wonderful contested mark in a pack 20m out from goal. He goes back and drills the set shot and the Suns lead is down to just four points. Cadman's got both of the Giants majors for the match. Meanwhile, Clayton Oliver is up to a game-high 16 disposals. He's having a sensational night so far. King flattened in big marking contest C By Chris De Silva A heart-in-mouth moment for Suns supporters as Ben King lays motionless on the turf after a big marking contest. Play continues with King sprawled out on the ground before the trainers are able to get to him. The good news is aside from a little bit of a limp, King is able to continue and doesn't even come off the ground for a check. Meanwhile, Leek Aleer is the latest Giant to miss a set shot, making the Giants 1.9 for the night. The scoreline is 0.3 to 0.2 for the quarter with 11 minutes left. It's safe to say we've not had Champagne Footy out here. Humphrey goes close on audacious banana C By Chris De Silva The Suns opening the second quarter with a couple of misses of their own to sit at 3.6. Bailey Humphrey the latest culprit, although you can't really blame him here as he hits the post with a set shot banana attempt from the boundary. That would've been a Goal of the Year contender, had he nailed it. Hogan strapped up after gnarly hand injury C By Chris De Silva GWS star Jesse Hogan had blood streaming from his right hand after splitting the webbing in a marking contest. The Giants have confirmed there is no structural damage to the hand, and Hogan's back out there to start the second quarter with his hand bandaged up. It'll be interesting to see how he goes trying to mark the footy with that on. QT: Gold Coast 3.4 (22) leads GWS Giants 1.7 (13) C By Chris De Silva Noah Anderson (left) kicked one of Gold Coast's three first-quarter goals. (Getty Images) It was a quarter of two halves really as the Suns dominating the first half of it before the Giants came storming back. We really looked set for a blow-out when the Suns kicked the first three goals of the match and had nine of the first 10 inside 50s of the match. GWS has gradually worked itself back into the contest and they've got seven of the last 10 scores. Unfortunately for them, most of them have been behinds. Gold Coast leads the inside 50 count 16-10, but GWS leads the clearance count 10-5, including an 8-2 edge around the ground. Suns defender John Noble is the leading ball-winner on the ground with 13 dipsosals, while Clayton Oliver is the high man for the Giants with 12. Oliver also has three clearances, three score involvements and two inside 50s. Christian Petracca was also excellent in that first term. He's got nine disposals (five contested), four score involvements and two clearances to go along with a goal. It's been a long weekend for everyone C By Chris De Silva Did commentator just say Robert Walls will be watching no doubt? He did VAD. - Melza Just for reference, Robert Walls died just under a year ago, so he will NOT in fact be watching Suns-Giants. Cadman breaks Giants drought with brilliant finish C By Chris De Silva Lovely transition from a back-half stoppage from the Giants as Finn Callaghan finds Aaron Cadman with a long cross-field kick. Callaghan's kick is basically a cut-out pass that takes out the entire Suns defence. Cadman, after marking around 70m out from goal, closes to 55m and drills it on the run. What a finish! The Giants have done well to hang around after that early Suns spurt. The margin back to just eight points now. The misses are piling up for the Giants C By Chris De Silva GWS definitely working its way back into this match, but they've got nothing to show for it just yet. Aaron Cadman and Stephen Coniglio both miss incredibly tough set shots from either pocket to leave the Giants at 0.5. GWS leads the clearance count 7-5 so far with Clayton Oliver already up to three himself. Hogan sprays set shot as GWS drought continues C By Chris De Silva The Giants are finally starting to get a few repeat inside 50 entries of their own now, mid-way into the first term. A lovely chain sees Jesse Hogan have a set shot directly in front from 35m out, but he badly sprays it. The Giants are 0.3 for the night so far, but the signs in the last couple of minutes have been a lot better. Anderson makes it three straight for the Suns C By Chris De Silva Gold Coast all over GWS like a cheap suit at the moment. World.title: To be frank, there’s no other store
World.content:
“So sad about the distress of David Jones,” writes Nola Tucker of Kiama. “My grandfather was a floorwalker there in the 1890s. ‘A man with the white carnation,’ said my mum. I also worked there on the ground floor in the Elizabeth Street store in Uni holidays and remember the excitement when Frank Sinatra was in Sydney and his bodyguard brought in a young Nancy to do some shopping.” Wonder if she bought any boots.

We’re putting an end to the thread concerning newbie torment (C8), as we’ve been advised by John Lees of Castlecrag that the topic “has been dealt with time and time again, and it’s the same old stories”. Gee, pretty sure we’ve covered fruit stickers in past as well. And indoor leaf blowers. Actually, I think we’re ok with that one.

That said, Dawn Glase of Moss Vale definitely blew it: “We have a dresser in our kitchen. The fluff and dust can’t be easily removed from under it. I got the bright idea of getting my husband to bring his leaf blower in to blow it out. Unfortunately, the stream of air went under the cupboard, up the back and blasted a decorative plate off the wall, smashing it to smithereens.”

Michael Fletcher of Greystanes reckons “George Zivkovic’s remarks about registration slogans (C8) bring to mind the many pointed slogans aimed at governments over the years (Singapore springs to mind) and NSW could well be ‘NSW - A Fine State’ given the penalties handed out for miscellaneous misdemeanours.”

Taking a practical approach is Janice Creenaune of Austinmer: “Why not make number plates a reminder to general driving rules and a way of living? ‘NSW - Back Off, Slow Down and Enjoy’.”

World.title: DCE heir apparent stars on debut but Panthers end Sea Eagles’ winning run
World.content:
Penrith 18 Manly 16 SportNRLNRL 2026 DCE heir apparent stars on debut but Panthers end Sea Eagles’ winning run Tom Decent May 3, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Manly’s bid for five straight wins under Kieran Foran since the sacking of Anthony Seibold fell agonisingly short on Sunday evening, as Penrith halfback Nathan Cleary orchestrated a hard-fought victory to secure the outright competition lead. Highly touted Manly halfback Joey Walsh was superb on his starting debut, setting up two tries in a gallant 18-16 defeat that offered a promising glimpse into the club’s future without stalwart Daly Cherry-Evans at the helm. Joey Walsh spots a hole in the Penrith defence on Sunday night. NRL Photos The 19-year-old’s stunning out-the-back, no-look pass to Haumole Olakau’atu before Ethan Bullemor’s try was the kind of moment that can ignite a career, underlining why there is so much hype around the former schoolboy rugby prodigy. “This is top-shelf ball play,” said premiership-winning halfback Cooper Cronk in commentary for Fox Sports. “He gets the ball … and tells an absolute lie with his eyes and his hips. That is a very good play by Joey Walsh.”



Walsh thrived in the absence of regular No.7 Jamal Fogarty, but Penrith found a way to surge past Manly after trailing 16-12 with 20 minutes remaining at CommBank Stadium. Walsh attempted a two-point field goal with just over a minute remaining but it fell well short. Panthers winger Brian To’o sinks his claws into Manly’s Ben Trbojevic. Getty Images Manly’s magnificent April has not quite carried into May, their four-game winning streak halted by a Panthers side that were far from perfect and turned over an uncharacteristic amount of ball. The Sea Eagles look an entirely different outfit to the slow-starting side of March. Whether Foran can maintain his early impact through the winter months remains to be seen, but to be within a try of the competition benchmark deep into the contest is an encouraging sign. A gorgeous cut-out pass from Cleary just before half-time restored Penrith’s advantage, with winger Brian To’o finishing in the right corner to hand the hosts a 12-6 lead at the break.



Foran was animated in the coaching box when Manly struck first through Clayton Faulalo, but the lead was short-lived as Penrith hit back through Blaize Talagi, who took the line on and delivered in the 10th minute. Penrith’s only slip-up of the season, against the Bulldogs last month, is almost a distant memory now, with Ivan Cleary’s side sharpening their focus as they build towards the Origin period sitting alone atop the ladder, two points clear of the Warriors, who have five wins from seven starts. View post on X On a weekend of injury concerns for NSW coach Laurie Daley — including Roosters duo Mark Nawaqanitawase (ankle) and Angus Crichton (knee) — Penrith’s stars emerged unscathed a fortnight out from the Blues squad announcement. Amid a flurry of high-scoring matches across the competition, the defensive resolve shown from both sides for the most part was refreshing to see.



There was drama early in the second half when Cleary claimed obstruction against Faulalo in the lead-up to Lehi Hopoate’s 52nd-minute try. Referee Wyatt Raymond acknowledged the contact but ruled it had no impact, to the frustration of Cleary, his teammates and Cronk, who declared it was “100 per cent no try”. The moment threatened to swerve Penrith off track in the second half before Izack Tago found the line and Cleary iced his third conversion from as many attempts to take what proved to be a match-winning two-point lead.

World.title: Injury-plagued Saint learns hamstring fate; Cripps avoids ban over ‘chicken-wing’ tackle
World.content:
AFL Briefing SportAFLAFL 2026 Injury-plagued Saint learns hamstring fate; Cripps avoids ban over ‘chicken-wing’ tackle Updated May 3, 2026 — 8:19pm ,first published 6:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

St Kilda’s Max King will be sidelined for some six weeks in the latest setback for the injury-plagued star forward. Scans on Sunday confirmed King had suffered a significant strain to his left hamstring. “The key forward is expected to spend approximately six weeks on the sidelines, with his return-to-play timeline to include a conditioning block,” a Saints statement read. The Saints, powered by an eight-goal third term, kicked a triple-figure tally for the fourth time this season in their 16.12 (108) to 9.15 (69) win over Carlton on Saturday night. It squared their win-loss record at 4-4, but coach Ross Lyon’s mood in the aftermath was tempered by news of King’s injury hours earlier.



The 25-year-old key forward, who hasn’t played at AFL level in almost two years, kicked two early goals in his second VFL game back from a calf issue. “I was watching it, he was looking good,” Lyon said. “I did speak about it during the week; that was the risk after such a long lay-off. “We’re trying to manage that soft tissue, so he’ll be disappointed, but he’s overcome bigger things.” AAP



Relief for Blues as Cripps avoids ban over ‘chicken-wing’ tackle Carlton captain Patrick Cripps has avoided a suspension for a chicken-wing tackle on St Kilda’s Hugo Garcia. Charged with misconduct, Cripps can instead accept a $1000 fine with an early guilty plea for his tackle on Garcia in the third quarter of Carlton’s 39-point loss to the Saints at Marvel Stadium on Saturday. Sanctions for the chicken-wing tackle have varied, with Fremantle forward Sam Switkowski banned for two matches for a tackle on then-Collingwood player Jack Ginnivan in 2022.



Former Richmond player Jack Riewoldt received a fine in 2019, but two-time Brownlow Medal winner Chris Judd served a four-week suspension in 2012 while playing for Carlton. Judd’s tackle on Leigh Adams left his North Melbourne opponent with a dislocated shoulder. Cripps’ tackle led to a fiery confrontation at Marvel Stadium with former Carlton teammate Jack Silvagni, who moved to the Saints with fellow high-profile recruit Tom De Koning. Patrick Cripps attempts to break a tackle against St Kilda. Getty Images Young Carlton defender Harry Dean was also charged with misconduct for shoving St Kilda’s Liam Ryan in the third quarter, and can accept the same sanction with an early guilty plea.



But Dean is expected to spend some time on the sidelines after picking up a groin issue, with scans to determine the extent of the damage. Garcia was also handed a $1000 fine for careless contact with an umpire in the second quarter. Elsewhere, West Coast youngster Elijah Hewett was slapped with a $3000 fine for striking Richmond’s Nick Vlastuin in the third quarter at Optus Stadium. World.title: Jeremy, 16, died from a tick-induced meat allergy. Sydney’s north is a global hotspot for the disease
World.content:
NationalIllness Jeremy, 16, died from a tick-induced meat allergy. Sydney’s north is a global hotspot for the disease Adam Hegarty and Anne Worthington May 3, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When he was 16, Jeremy Webb went on a Central Coast camping trip with friends. They ate sausages and marshmallows. Feeling breathless and nauseous, he ran for help, but collapsed. His friends called an ambulance as they desperately tried to resuscitate him. Jeremy Webb, 16, died from anaphylaxis due to Mammalian Meat Allergy. 60 Minutes He died that night at Gosford Hospital. His parents were told Jeremy had a fatal attack of asthma, a condition he had suffered since a young child. But the explanation didn’t sit right. “It was just one of those things where you just don’t have a 16-year-old just drop dead,” his mother Myfanwy told 60 Minutes. In February the NSW Deputy Coroner agreed, and concluded that Jeremy’s cause of death was not asthma but anaphylaxis due to Mammalian Meat Allergy, which is caused by ticks and triggers a reaction to red meat, pork or any other product from a mammal. Sydney’s northern beaches and the Central Coast have become global hotspots for the disease, which Australia’s national science agency, the CSIRO, warns is on the rise and a “significant health concern”.



The link between Mammalian Meat Allergy and the Eastern Paralysis tick was discovered by immunologist and allergy physician Professor Sheryl Van Nunen in 2007, after dozens of patients on the northern beaches began presenting with life-threatening allergic reactions in the middle of the night. Using the contents from their last meal, she did a skin test and found a reaction to mammalian meat or a derived product. She also discovered her patients had something else in common – bites from the Eastern Paralysis tick. “So I’m thinking if the ticks are a parasite and the people have developed the meat allergy that hasn’t been happening in the last 20 years I’ve been here, then clearly there’s something new going on,” she told 60 Minutes (which is broadcast by Nine, the owner of this masthead). Jeremy Webb was five when his family moved to their property on the Central Coast, a natural playground for a boy who loved the beach and bush. He’d spend hours in his outdoor cubby with his dog Wasp. As he got older, he built trails to ride his bike. Myfanwy first noticed Jeremy was getting bitten by ticks from when he was about seven. By 10, he had started feeling “queasy” after eating red meat or pork. He became so sensitised that even the fumes from cooking them could make him feel unwell.



Myfanwy and Jonathan Webb, whose 16-year-old son Jeremy died from Mamalian Meat Allergy. 60 Minutes The symptoms persisted after Jeremy stopped eating red meat and pork; his eyes would be swollen and he’d often wake up through the night struggling to breathe. His parents assumed it was his asthma. Related Article Explainer

Allergies What is anaphylaxis – and what should you do if someone has an attack? “The problem is when your kid has asthma and they wake up with nocturnal asthma, you don’t know the difference,” his father, Jonathan, said. “And that was certainly the case for us because I do remember once Jeremy woke up and we were giving him his Ventolin and he said, ‘It’s not working’.” The Webbs had heard of Mammalian Meat Allergy or Alpha Gal Syndrome, but were not aware that it could be lethal or that symptoms could be brought on by consuming not just meat or pork, but any other product derived from a mammal such as dairy and gelatin.



Jonathan said he now thinks his son’s nighttime attacks were triggered by dairy. “Jeremy was still eating things like ice-cream, which could clearly trigger a reaction,” he said. “I suspect some of the nocturnal asthma might have been a response to eating ice-cream because he loved his ice-cream.” It wasn’t just the Webbs who were unaware of the allergy’s potential deadly consequences. In the years leading up to Jeremy’s death, he was admitted twice to Gosford Hospital with symptoms of anaphylaxis. On both occasions, the possibility was overlooked. Doctors said the likely culprit was his asthma and Jeremy was discharged without further investigation. Jonathan believes the hospital admissions were missed opportunities. “We should have gone home with an EpiPen and a letter of management that we needed to go and see an allergy specialist, but that was never done,” he said. “And unfortunately on the Central Coast, the paramedics, the doctors, the GPs didn’t know about [meat allergy]. And I want that to change.”



The allergy involves a reaction to a carbohydrate called alpha-galactose, which is found in the meat of all mammals but not in humans. Mammalian Meat Allergy is caused by ticks and triggers an allergy to red meat, pork or any other product derived from a mammal. 60 Minutes It is also found in the saliva of ticks. When the tick is disturbed while feeding, it injects its saliva, causing the immune system to make antibodies to fight the foreign presence. Van Nunen said after two tick bites, 50 per cent of people will make allergy antibodies to the alpha-gal molecule. Van Nunen identified this antibody in blood samples taken from Jeremy Webb during his autopsy. “The forensic pathologist had put aside some blood from Jeremy, and that was tested, and we were able to make the diagnosis,” she said.



Her evidence at the inquest into Jeremy’s death was critical. The teenager was the first documented death from MMA in Australia, but she suspects there have been more. “I know more people have died from this. People who’ve been categorised as their mode of death being asthma where it’s actually been food allergy.” Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Hope for people with mysterious and debilitating tick bite symptoms MMA, though rare, is on the rise. A soon-to-be published report by the CSIRO for the first time documents the number of cases of the condition in Australia and maps hotspots along the east coast. Dr Alex Gofton, the study lead, said the findings were a significant health concern. “There’s over 5000 people living with this condition,” he said. “We also found that, unfortunately, case numbers are on the rise. Since 2020, case numbers have increased 22 per cent year-on-year, which is a really concerning trend.”



Van Nunen hopes the finding into Jeremy’s death will compel governments to act. Since 2013, the federal and state government have been asked to produce “an effective campaign pitched somewhere between the Grim Reaper and Slip, Slop and Slap, warning people of the problems that tick bites can cause and teaching them how to deal with tick bites”. The Webb family hopes the tragedy of Jeremy’s death will lead to greater awareness about MMA, among the public and medical profession alike, and a lesson on prevention. “If we’d known, my son would still be here today. I’m 100 per cent sure of that,” Jonathan said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: When tension is a good thing: Meet the acrobat couple running a circus
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life When tension is a good thing: Meet the acrobat couple running a circus Carolyn Webb May 3, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As a couple who run a circus, Charice Rust and Jonathan Morgan have learned the importance of work-life balance. In the past decade, the Melbourne pair have juggled home life with touring the world in their acrobatic troupe, One Fell Swoop. It’s taken time, and practice, to perfect. I’ve got you: Jonathan Morgan and Charice Rust in rehearsal with their One Fell Swoop Circus. Chris Hopkins “We had to learn some boundaries, like try not to ask the other person, ‘have you done that thing you needed to do’ at 11pm, before going to sleep,” Morgan says. “We’re pretty good at that now.” Tension, however, can be a force for good, they say.



It’s one of the themes behind their new show, In Common, that the couple and four other acrobats will perform at the South Side Festival in Frankston next Saturday. In the show, the troupe work together to build an apparatus, resembling giant pick-up sticks from poles and cables, and demonstrate gravity-defying feats on it, involving trust and risk. Loading Morgan says: “It’s about those invisible safety nets and the lines of tension that holds communities together. And the way that, once you build those structures, you can flourish within them.” He says participants might feel they can take risks, and be caught if they fall, such as the audience might also feel if they take a stand on an issue in the community.



Lives entwined: Charice Rust and Jonathan Morgan performing their show, By a Thread, at Castlemaine State Festival in 2021. Shane Carey Morgan and Rust went out on a limb by founding One Fell Swoop in 2016 after they both graduated from the National Institute of Circus Arts in Prahran. To date, the circus has performed everywhere from Canada to China, and in August, they will perform for the second time at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival. Morgan and Rust say they have complementary skills in running the circus: Morgan is a mechatronics engineer who until recently – as well as performing in the circus – worked on the University of Melbourne’s SpIRIT satellite project. Rust says Morgan is “better at budgets, numbers, engineering and rigging, and I look after tour co-ordination, the artists and relationship building”.



While Rust gained an arts degree before NICA, she has been acrobatic since childhood. On visits to her family’s farm in western Victoria, Rust would stand on her uncle’s shoulders, do handstands on tractors, and walk along fence-tops. Stage of life: Charice Rust and partner Jonathan Morgan. Chris Hopkins She says making a living in the arts is not easy, but working with your partner can help. “Rehearsal days are long and hard,” Rust says. “I know that when I’m running out of words and energy, Jonathan can take over.



“Just having someone there to do it all with is amazing,” Rust says. Testing new concepts and moves for a show takes courage, as well as trial and error. “So having your partner, someone you trust, that you can share that with is pretty incredible,” Rust said. One Fell Swoop Circus will perform twice on Saturday, May 9, at 1pm and at 7.30pm, at Frankston Arts Centre. The South Side Festival is on from May 8 to 17 in Frankston.
